utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we begin in the usual manner by having today's appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. On behalf of the Prosecution I'm Tom Hannis with our case manager, Jasmina Bosnjakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Stanisic's Defence team, Slobodan Cvijetic and Eugene O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Igor Pantelic and Dragan Krgovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, are you ready to continue with your examination-in-chief of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I may address one thing before we bring in the witness. Following the suggestion from the Bench yesterday, I identified some 14 documents that are in the nature of dispatches, outgoing dispatches from CSB Banja Luka, they seem to be regular in form. I provided a list to the Chamber and to Defence to see if Defence had any objection to me moving to tender those en masse, as it were. I've heard from Mr. Krgovic. I understand that he doesn't have an objection, but I haven't heard yet from Mr. Cvijetic and Zecevic team or Mr. Stanisic as to their position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we wish to express our reservations and put our objection on the record, and this is due to our standpoint regarding the contents of these documents -- I do apologise. The joint standpoint of all the Defence teams is that we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So it merely remains a matter of organisation and mechanics as to how you -- how these are marked and put onto the record, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would propose to tender them. The list has been submitted to the Registry. They're in chronological order. I should note that on the list we provided yesterday, number 7, which is a document dated 29 May 1992, it was 65 ter 0144, was admitted yesterday as Exhibit P1007. This was the fax document. I jumped to it because the witness had mentioned fax and so I jumped to it to use it as an example. So it does not need a new number. It's on the list as number 7, that should be ignored, but the others if we could start with the next number in line and just number them sequentially that would be -- I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Registry will deal with those documents accordingly. Thank you. Could the usher please escort the witness back to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I understand by the calculation I have perhaps five minutes left. I would like to request an additional 20 minutes or so to finish-up with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do I correctly --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- do I correctly read that the present schedule anticipates this witness carrying over into Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess based on the estimated time for Defence cross-examination, that's likely to happen. I don't know if their estimated time has changed now or not, but I think the previous indication was they had about five hours between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It will certainly be less than that, so I think we will complete this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before Mr. Hannis resumes his examination-in-chief of you, I would remind you that you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rakovic. Yesterday I had shown you a document that was the report for the first six months of 1992 on the work of your centre in Banja Luka. I'd next like to show you Exhibit P621. This is a document dated October 1992, and it purports to be the report on the work of the centre in Banja Luka for the period from 1 July through 30 September 1992. Do you remember being shown a part of this document during your proofing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 31 in the English, and I think in e-court it's also 31 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, this is section 5.1 on the functioning of the system of communications and crypto protection. Are you able to read that paragraph on your screen?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see it indicates that during this three-month time-period there were 1.996 non-coded dispatches and 152 coded received, while there were 1385 non-coded dispatches and 43 coded dispatches that had been sent or delivered. I don't know if you recall the six-month report, but I think the numbers were more in the neighbourhood of 9.000. Do you remember that the number was much higher during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that it was 9.600 in that report. I saw that yesterday during my proofing. I also saw this during my proofing, this number of 1.900 and whatever it says here. Well, even during the proofing I said that something was not clear to me. As this is an excerpt from that report, it ought to refer to this three-month period evidently. And if we look at the six-month period where it's 9.500, the portion is 1:2 or 2.5. And I really couldn't say whether this report as it was written was correct or whether the number of dispatches actually decreased. I really couldn't say what happened. Perhaps this is information referring to one month because we had three-month periods, six-month periods, and so on. It might have been a typing error or maybe somebody copied the figures for just one month by mistake instead of the three-month period because this is really a far smaller number of dispatches compared with the number in the other report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree with you about the difference in the number, but you as head of that section, wouldn't you be responsible for this information that's being put in the three-month report for the centre? And you're saying you think the information is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is that it's possible that this is a report referring to a period of just one month. Perhaps the figures were switched by mistake, because according to this it would seem that this was the number of dispatches for the entire period covered by the report. I was responsible, but I could have made a mistake. It's also possible that the number of dispatches decreased. I can't assert whether this is due to a decrease in the number of dispatches or to an error in reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, you're still in the same job you had back in 1992, and I assume that's because you're competent at your job. This report says it's for a three-month period. Now, assume for a minute, if you will, that the numbers are correct, isn't it possible that the reason for the big decrease in numbers during this three-month time-period is because after the 1st of July, relatively speaking, things in terms of organisation in the MUP have improved since the beginning of the year and certainly since April. So things have calmed down. There isn't a need to send so many dispatches. Perhaps other means of communications like the phone lines are working better, fax machines are working. That could be a reason for a decrease in dispatches, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's obviously a leading question. The answer is very simple. I can clarify that in cross, Your Honour, but what the Prosecution suggests, I mean, it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand you, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Hannis, before Mr. Krgovic's intervention, it struck me as an odd question having regard to the, perhaps not clear, but the answer that the witness had, in fact, given to the earlier question, the -- it's really a question that's asked and answered. I -- the question that you just phrased which Mr. Krgovic objected struck me more as an argument that you're making with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps I phrased it badly. What the witness had said was one possibility is that the information in the report is wrong and it's only for one month instead of three months. But he conceded the possibility the information is correct and that there was a big decrease. I guess my question should be:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If those numbers in the report are correct, why do you think the numbers have decreased to such a significant extent? Do you understand my question, Mr. Rakovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question, but it's very hard for me to answer because I didn't write dispatches and have 500 dispatches in my book for the first three months and a hundred for the second three. I would have observed that something had changed and the number had decreased, but all I can say here is that there are these two possibilities. There's also a third possibility, which I didn't mention and which has arisen now, and that's perhaps that the number of dispatches decreased. So one possibility is that the number of dispatches decreased because this information might be erroneous, it might refer only to the last month. Because as I said, we drew up or compiled reports for three-month periods --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let me stop you there. I think you've answered the question, and you're repeating your earlier answer, so let me go on to something else. I would like to show you Exhibit 65 ter 3189.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Excuse me, the previous documents, I don't seem to be able to find it on your list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: P621 is one of the two documents that I referred to in a separate mail --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In a separate mail, oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My apologies. I should have alerted you to that. I understand we're looking for 65 ter 3189.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: While we're looking for that, let me just ask you a general question about dispatches. In the telegraph or Teletype documents I see sometimes, for example, Mr. Zupljanin's name spelled with Z-z at the beginning of his name or if we saw Mr. Stanisic's name it might be spelled S-t-a-n-i and then there would be s-s and i-c-c. I understand that duplication of certain consonants is because there's no way to put the diacritic in a Teletype. Do you understand? Am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have the same assumption as you. These signs -- the letters that have diacritics, they are doubled usually. I noticed that as well. That's how it was set up on the machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand that 65 ter 3189 is a -- there's a duplicate which is 65 ter 3100. That may be the one that's in e-court. I understand it's the same ERN, and if we could bring that up I hope that's the one I'm trying to show the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You have a 50 per cent chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I hope I'm lucky today, Your Honour. That appears to be it. And if we could go to page 3 of the document in the B/C/S. I'm sorry, I need to go one more, page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, do you recall having taken a look at this particular log-book during your interview and/or during proofing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I may, because it's a big document, Your Honours, could I hand him a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall having looked at it before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a day or two ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for purposes of getting to 1992, if we could go to the -- I think it's approximately page 100 in e-court. And for you, Mr. Rakovic, you see the -- you see the eight-digit number stamped at the top, if you could go to the one that ends in the last four digits of 2268, 2268. So it's about 40 or 50 pages on for you. Can you tell us what this appears to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the page in English I think is 15, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of log-book this is?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the book of incoming dispatches. Dispatches which arrived and were received in our centre were entered into this book. CSB Banja Luka and I don't know from whom. So I do apologise, this -- it says here: To whom it was addressed, from whom and for whom. So sender and addressee. So it should be the Prijedor SJB and the sender, I see it's CSB Banja Luka mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Column 9 is to whom the listed documents are addressed, and I see almost all those appear to be 11-12, which I think you confirmed for me yesterday would be the SJB in Prijedor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, based on what I saw in all these other documents, 11-12, we didn't go on and put 01 and so on, but by this other figure, 12, in my opinion to the best of my knowledge, that ought to refer to Prijedor from my previous experience and the documents I've seen so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could look near the bottom of the page in the far left column are simply sequential numbers. So would you look at 395, and for that --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- one we see in column 4 that 395 was a telegram and the number was 11-115. That would be a document from your centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that we actually saw it yesterday at one point, I think, as a document, separate document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would indicate that 11-15 [sic] is the number carried on Exhibit P553 in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 397 is document number 11-119. Again that's a document from the Banja Luka security service -- security services centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is just like 395. It -- it's the same thing, 11-119, and up there it was 11-115.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I would indicate that 11-119, is the number carried on Exhibit P1002 introduced yesterday. I have other examples, but at this point I would move to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1025, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And lastly, the last thing I want to show you, Mr. Rakovic, is 65 ter 2399. I think this is one you've seen before, it's a sort of schematic diagram of I think the telephone links in the MUP before the war began in April 1992. And if we could -- on the B/C/S document if we could zoom in on the upper left quadrant. Yes. That's good. Do you recall looking at this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't exactly remember; however, this is familiar as soon as I see it. As soon as I see it, I know roughly what it's got to be. It says here, Survey of the Organs of the Interior. That's what it was called, internal telephone special network, that's what it says, right, because the centres are depicted here and the police stations -- or rather, the public security stations that were linked up within that former system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And the legend I have says that the circle with a small circle inside that we see for Banja Luka indicates a nodal switchboard. Am I using the correct term?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, sort of -- yes, well nodal switchboard, if I can put it that way, you can see here Jajce and -- it is like -- well, not a final point -- I don't know how to call this. This is not exactly my forte, but it was -- well, Prijedor was linked to Banja Luka and then from Prijedor these municipalities as depicted here, just like Jajce, Sipovo, Mrkonjic, it was sort of a sub system, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a specific question. We see a link between Banja Luka and Prijedor, and then from Prijedor there are links to Sanski Most, Novi, and Dubica. It appears that there was not a direct telephone link from Banja Luka to Sanski Most. Was that the situation in 1992, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this diagram, it seems that that is the way it was. I mean, I could not remember. This primarily relates to the internal special network that the ministry of the then-Bosnia-Herzegovina had. As I've said, when I arrived I didn't even have time to read up or anything. There were already cuts, and I don't remember whether there was a direct link. However, I remember the directories that we had, so then we had the codes how you could call Jajce, Mrkonjic, et cetera. However, by the time I was supposed to use it, half of it was cut off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Policemen -- or rather, there were all sorts of things going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you there. I saw in one document a reference to a coded telephone line. Were you aware if in 1992 in CSB Banja Luka there was a secure phone line or a coded phone line? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that that was in Banja Luka in 1992 when I got there, but people were saying -- I mean, colleagues who worked there, that beforehand there had been this one line between Banja Luka and the Sarajevo MUP. And, in fact, that was cut off immediately. There were some protection devices, but anyway it was only the chiefs of the centres and the minister who could have that kind of link, the republican minister at the time actually. I mean, I meant the minister of the then-Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's what I meant. However, as far as I know, no one ever mentioned that line, and no one ever used it. In fact, I didn't know of it, and there weren't any interventions on our part in terms of doing something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. My last question has to do with your -- any communications or co-ordination you had with the -- with MUP at the republic level. Did you know a Dragan Kezunovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dragan Kezunovic was my chief of administration up until -- say, until 2000, so for about eight years. I think he was pensioned off then, temporarily. He became an advisor to the minister, I don't know who the minister was at the time, and then he was pensioned off, and he was the chief of administration after Sabic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In 1992 when you were working in Banja Luka, was he your superior in your line of work?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Dragan Kezunovic in my line of work at that time. I'm sorry, when I got there, I got there on the 1st of April. So when I got there Akif Sabic was my superior in my line of work. But then when the joint Ministry of the Interior fell apart, when the Ministry of the Interior of the Serb Republic was established, then Kezunovic was my boss. But in the interim period from the 1st of April until I don't know what date, then Akif Sabic was my boss. I was actually supposed to go to some meeting up there and nobody went and after the first conversations we had, I didn't really speak to him afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then after the creation of the RS MUP, Mr. Kezunovic was your superior for the rest of 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that time. When the MUP of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, later Republika Srpska, up until about 2000 Dragan Kezunovic was my superior in my line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just give me a few minutes to organise my stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Rakovic. We met the other day briefly, but for the record my name is Dragan Krgovic, and on behalf of the Defence of Stojan Zupljanin I'm going to put some questions to you today in relation to your testimony. As opposed to the Prosecutor, you and I speak the same language so I would like to ask you to listen to my question carefully and then pause briefly before you start answering. Mr. Rakovic, I'm going to take you back to a topic that you discussed with the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could the witness please be shown P545. Could we have it in e-court, please. That is page 17 in the Serbian version. Could we see the first page first. If I understand it correctly, it's P545, or do I have the right marking actually? Just a second, please. Maybe it's a mistake. No, it's 595. Sorry. Sorry. My case manager writes 4s and 9s very similarly, so ... This is the right document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, please have a look at this. This is a report on the work of the security services centre from the 1st of January until the 30th of June, 1992, and you talked about it to the Prosecutor. It covers a peace time-period, if we can put it that way, January, February, March, and part of April, and then the period when the war conflicts broke out. So there is about three or three and a half months of peace and normal functioning, and you have about two and a half months of war operations in that period. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that roughly that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And on page 17 there --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 17 actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Last paragraph a certain number is given -- sorry, 03246781 is the ERN number. I've just been told now that the page numbers do not correspond to the ones in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] I think in e-court it's page number 18 because the cover page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last paragraph in the B/C/S version. In the English version it's the next page, the one after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, on the basis of this I infer that this is the total number of dispatches from that period of peace and from that period of war; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it should be, six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So in the next report up until September you have those three months, you are only dealing with a period of war, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that due to all of these problems that were there in your work, there were less dispatches in the period of war than in the period of peace, isn't that right, that's only logical, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it seems. However, we have a problem here. We need to have a clear-cut distinction between one period of three months and another period of three months; however, there is no such thing. This way we fall into a trap. 9.000 for six months and 2.000 for three months, and we don't know whether there were 5.000 in the first three months or 7.000 or whatever, that's quite possible too. I mean, these are just possibilities, options, assumptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that in a situation of war telegraphic and teleprinter traffic was seriously impeded, which is only logical, so not the same number of dispatches were sent in peacetime and in war time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree on that. This number of dispatches presented here went through our service only. There is a possibility of this number being lower because some of the communication did not go through our service. So perhaps that's the reason for the decrease -- it may be one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You will see, as my learned friend Mr. Hannis said, the ratio in this period is such that in percentage terms there are two and a half times less dispatches in wartime than in peacetime; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In -- here we see that it seems to be two and a half times less -- I mean compared to the first six months if we look at the percentages by months, on average.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That could be due to war operations and the inability to have proper communication by teleprinter, telegraph, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It also could have been due to a smaller number of dispatches going through us and the fact that we were not able to deliver them all to the proper addresses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, at the very outset -- well, now we've had this clarification and this was the last topic that we discussed. However, now chronologically I'm going to go back to the same order of topics that the Prosecutor dealt with. You said that you came to this position on the 1st of April, 1992, if I understood you properly?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you went through all of those conversations at the MUP -- or rather, tests at the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that happened in Sarajevo, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I went three times there for medical examinations, interviews. Once I didn't manage to do anything. I had to wait all day and nothing. And once I went for a medical examination, so I think I went three times from 1991 onwards for these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, you started working on the 1st of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you started working there in that department, you mentioned that there were quite a few Muslims and Croats who were employed there, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I started that job I found the people who had been working there. That's the way it was. I can say that the service was headed by a Croat, and he retired around new year or at the end of September in 1991. But at any rate, I know that by the 31st of December, 1991, he had already retired, the Croat --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Was it 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1992, when I came. But I'm just saying now in addition to that that in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... for the interpreters to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You heard Judge Hall. Perhaps we should slow down a bit, both you and I, Rakovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I got there on the 1st of April, the head of the maintenance department was Stipo Ojdanic, a Croat. Mustafa Hasanovic was chief engineer, he was a Muslim or a Bosniak as it's now called. The chief of the department for crypto protection was Zika Hadziselimovic, Zijad, a Bosniak. The communications officer was a Bosniak. Then Milos Sakic, a Croat, was working in maintenance. When I arrived -- now, was it in May or the end of May, Zeljo Sabic, a Croat, got a job there. I think he started working with us in the beginning of June, and he worked with us throughout the war, I mean, all the time. Babic Robert, a Croat, he also started working on the 1st of April, but then since he was not on the list of reservists he was on the list of the army, he went to the Army of Republika Srpska as a signals person. So then he went there, but during the first period he worked here too. So in the department where I worked, both the professionals and those, I mean who had been working there up until then, had different ethnic backgrounds. That is what I can say for sure. I can give you all the names as well. As far as I know, all those people were there in 1991, all of 1992. I think that Stipo and Mustafa actually retired on the 31st of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No one asked you to discharge these people or not to admit the Croat you referred to, as far as your department was concerned you have the right to propose on the basis of professional criteria who was supposed to work with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. There was a storage of personnel anyway and some people had retired. When I got there it was very favourable to retire in 1991/1992. So people retired then, quite a few people retired then and they got good pensions, so when I got there, there were quite a few vacancies, and we had a shortage of personnel. What I tried to do then was to return some people from the reserve force. I also talked to people about their ethnic backgrounds to come and work there as reservists. They were a bit skeptical. Others came, for instance. For example, Sunkic we mentioned him yesterday. He started working straight away. Bojic Milorad, he started working as a pensioner. Trmosljanin Milan, a pensioner as well. They were all asked to come in and work. Professor Dr. Kolonic Dzemal was asked to come and help us because he was highly professional. The dean of the faculty of electrical engineering actually sent a request not to ask him to come and work for us because they wanted to keep him at the university, and then we agreed to that. The professor works at the faculty of electrical engineering to this day. That is what I'd like to say in relation to the personnel employed in the department where I was. Let me tell you one more thing. At the same time, I tried to find out where there were professionals who could work with us. I found a few people who worked for the railways and the telecoms, and so on in Rudi Cajavec as well, so I found some people and they were asked to come and join us. Personnel affairs were my very own line of work in my department. I could make proposals who should be employed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The last gentleman you spoke of, Professor Dzemal Konjevic, he's a Muslim, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Bosniak, yes, hails from Prijedor. He completed his own studies in Banja Luka and stayed on in Banja Luka, and he was a minister in the Government of Republika Srpska during the term of the last government, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Some of the names are not in the transcript, the names of the persons you found when you first started working there. There were Muslims and Croats, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Dzemal Kolonic is his name, not Konjevic. So could the transcript please be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We have two answers recorded. The persons we mentioned were Croats and Muslims and your answer was yes -- and they rest you said about Mr. Kolonic --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to have his last name changed because it was not recorded correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I thought. Mr. Rakovic, how should I put this, you needed people -- for example, you needed a teleprinter operator and they'd bring someone and then you would see that he was not really well-versed in this line of work and he you would take him in -- he was already there, rather. And then say another organ, they did not meet professional requirements. And then especially some of these people from the reserve force, say they had committed some violations beforehand. So, in fact, they would come by way of war assignment in the MUP or the CSB, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would get war assignment, and those people who received war assignments would be received there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And if you would want -- well, not you specifically but other people too. I mean for certain reasons, say because of lack of discipline or some things that previously happened in their lives, or say if they had a record beforehand, then these people would not remain there, their war assignment would not remain the same, you would send them back to the Ministry of Defence and then.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would happen. I can tell you about what happened in my service. Say a man was taken in to work with Milos Sakic on maintaining the switchboard because it was not enough to have just one person working for 24 hours. He came from the Bosna Hotel. He worked on telephone maintenance at the Bosna Hotel. He worked in my service for a month. He was a good man, he wasn't a criminal, he wasn't a thief or anything, but he was not interested in his work. He was not a good person for my service. He could not meet the requirements. I wanted someone who would be extremely agile, who would be there day and night, if necessary, to work. So since I had brought him, in fact, I said, "Sir, it would be best for us to go our separate ways like civilised human beings," and he signed a statement saying that he was leaving that job and thereby his war assignment stopped and his service with us as well, if I can put it that way. So it is only natural that afterwards he got a different war assignment or got a different job, whatever, but it is only natural that a person who would bring someone in would talk to that person if there was a problem. I mean, I don't want to have any problems created. I mean, he didn't want to initiate any kind of proceedings or something, so yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And at the level of the Banja Luka CSB, who were the people dealing with personnel and recruiting new employees, who did most of the recruiting of employees, police officers, and so on for the CSB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was mostly people in the human resources department. Mane Popovic I think was there for a while. I think that for police work it was even the chief of the police department, Djuro Bulic. He is deceased now. And that's to the best of my knowledge. That's what people said. They brought quite a lot of people to be reserve officers to bring the force up to manpower level. And this had to do with telephone conversations, people asking for help, personal friendships. That was my opinion because I thought that quite a few of the people who arrived in this way were problematic. When I got my job, I spent the whole day being checked, going through medical checks, psychological checks to prove that I was a normal person able to do that job. But then at that time nobody examined those people or checked them as far as I know. For the most part, they arrived just like that, the reservists I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And if it was established that these people did not meet certain criteria or had problems with discipline, then those people who had brought them there would send them back to the Ministry of Defence or put them at the disposal of the army; is that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, where I was working and from what I was able to see, that's how it was. There was a story going around -- for example, I've sent him back to Vojo Dinic, that's what he would say, and Vojo Dinic was in charge of assigning people their wartime assignment, and he was in charge of recruitment for the army for military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you were asked by the OTP about the disciplinary commission, you explained how issues of lack of discipline were dealt with in your view, simply by being sent back to Vojo Dinic, is that it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, when answering the Prosecutor's questions yesterday you spoke about the communications system, and you mentioned UKT stations and mobile stations. So just a question. These UKT devices were not used for communication between the CSB and the SJBs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: UKT traffic could be used, but the operative duty service had a station it could use to contact any station on the territory of the CSB. Because they had a stationary UKT station in their office, they still have it, and they sent messages via the repeater. But most of this traffic was of local nature for the needs of mobile police patrols in towns and maybe patrols doing their beat on foot in villages and towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Because this has a short range, this kind of device?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the ones that used a repeater via Kozara, they could use both stations in cars and stationary ones; but with the small device that we had you couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: During his examination-in-chief, the Prosecutor asked you quite a lot of questions about the functioning of the communications system, and I'm interested in what happened at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we still have Exhibit P595 on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read it carefully. That's the page that's open now. Just a moment. Could you just explain one point. You -- I will read out a sentence to you. "In view of the security situation, the reduced number of professionals, the lack of fuel, it was not possible to -- to checks in the SJBs, but mostly we focused on removing breakdowns, repairing breakdowns, and placing stations where there had been none before." So you mentioned the Donji Vakuf SJB, Bosanska Krupa, and Kupres, which means that there had been no communication with those stations and that you were actually setting up communications with them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And secondly, due to combat activities there were constant interruptions of telephone and telegraph communications in the SJBs. You mentioned the Kupres, Donji Vakuf, Bosanska Krupa, Glamoc, Bihac, Teslic, Bosanski Grahovo, Drvar, Sipovo, Mrkonjic Grad, and others. I understand that there were constant interruptions with these stations I mentioned and others; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. In this first part I said that there had been interruptions in communications, but I didn't mention the stations that were close to Banja Luka because we went there to repair things and improve things. Now you've read out a larger number of stations. Donji Vakuf, Krupa, Kupres, there were no communications with them. I said that we went to Kupres several times and tried to get some sort of number where the police could at least report from a -- on a daily basis. There was a president of a municipality there, I don't recall his name, and together with a man from the PTT we tried to say, "Well, let's set up at least one line so that we from the police can use it sometimes, go there to make a call, and so on." And this large number of stations, all of them used to belong to other larger centres, such as Livno, Bihac, or Jajce, and as this was cut off there automatically special communications and telegraph communications were cut off as well, and we were trying to establish communications there, set something up. There was power cut also no electricity. So Gradiska, Knezevo, Laktasi, those were places where we were constantly having problems. We would have electricity, they would not have it. There was a period when there was a power cut in Banja Luka for two months. I went down to the post office, they had two generators of 250 Kilo-watts each, so they managed -- they barely managed to keep going maintaining the minimum of telephone communications. That's why I said that it was very difficult with constant interruptions and sometimes it would take a comes man a whole day to send a dispatch to one station, and he would say to his colleague: I've managed to send these but not those. These are some police stations I couldn't reach, so you try to do it. That's what I meant when I said there had been constant interruptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, on page 87 you told the Prosecutor that when it came to Donji Vakuf it was in your communications system, but you had no contact with Donji Vakuf at all?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to remember everything, but that was a sort of isolated oasis. Sometimes when I spoke to some people who used to arrive from there they had their own routes, their own means of reaching Banja Luka. They didn't use the regular roads. They went through forests and over mountains. There was no normal communication as there was with stations closer to Banja Luka because Donji Vakuf used to be part of another CSB, not Banja Luka. That's why those communications had not been set up earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just jog your memory. At that time in that area Jajce was in the hands of the Muslim and Croat forces, and that was where the communications went?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The main road went through Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So quite logically the communications line went along the same route?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I suppose that's how it was. I can't know every detail about where the lines went. There were cables up in the air, so it was possible to cut them. Those cables that went towards Vakuf and further on towards Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And now I'll take you back to the previous, or rather, I'll take you to the next sentence. "In spite of these difficulties, bearing in mind the power cuts, the lack of fuel for generators, the fact that the generator batteries are spent, which is all introducing chaos into the communications situation, especially in telegraphic communications." So this is what the situation was at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, based on all of this I see clearly now that the number of dispatches was reduced in the second and the third quarter. If we could see the overview for the first quarter, then we would have the complete picture of what the situation was as regards sending dispatches.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you a document, P160. Mr. Rakovic, this is a summary from a meeting held in Belgrade in July. I believe you didn't know about that meeting or about this document, but if we could look at page 5 of this document. I do apologise. Could we first have page 2 so we can see who the speaker is. Here Stojan Zupljanin is describing the situation on the territory of the Banja Luka CSB. I just wanted to show you this, and then let's look at page 5 and in English, it's page 8. In e-court it's 03241855 ERN. The last paragraph on this page. Here Stojan Zupljanin says: "The functional communications system has been destroyed. There have been talks with representatives of Rudi Cajavec about acquisition of equipment." Do you agree that this corresponds to what you wrote in your report that this is what the situation was in 1992 in those wartime months?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with that. We are now talking about the functional system, and the functional system consisted of four subsystems. When we talk about the functional system of communications, it was practically destroyed. We only had parts of the subsystem, which sometimes worked and sometimes didn't. If the telephone system is a special communications system, special telephone lines, I'm not saying that it's something special. It's just a closed telephone system with a very shortened way of dialling, so that's why people thought it was special. It was simply an internal telephone system just as we now have the internet, which is a global system, and some services have their intranet, which is the internal system. You might have your own intranet here as well. That's what it was. So we say that the functional system had been destroyed. From 1991 onwards, everyone tried to grab as much as they could for themselves, and nothing was invested in new equipment. Everybody thought well the next person to come to power will do the investing. So no batteries, stations, vehicles, generators were bought. And when I arrived, I was the first to feel the consequences because when you come to work you pick up a telephone and its dead. Well, it's as if it wasn't there. So to this very day when somebody calls me up and says, "Rakovic, why is my telephone not working?" I said, "Well, mine isn't working either, it's not working because it's not working. The switchboard is out of order." So work has to be done on putting it in order. It has to be fixed. I didn't have batteries for the existing stations, there were no new stations. The chief of the centre and Cajavec went to see Dragan together, to see if there were any spare parts that might be used to maintain the stationary stations, the ones in cars, the hand-held stations. I tried to get hold of anything I could. We tried to establish contacts to procure equipment. We even managed to get a hundred stations through Sarajevo, but somebody stole even those in Sarajevo. We had held Motorolas -- we had Motorolas, a hundred, 200 type Motorolas that we managed to get. The teleprinter system had been destroyed. Before we used to take teleprinters to Sarajevo to be repaired, and from Sarajevo they would take them to Nis, but that was now all destroyed. There was nobody who could fix things, who could repair them, and that's probably what I told the chief when I briefed him. I said, "I don't know what to do." We know how to do the job but we can't do it. If I'm new here and there are things I don't know, that's possible, but Musa and this other guy who have been there for 20 years, he worked there throughout the war, an exceptional able engineer, all those lads there, well they couldn't do anything either because they didn't have anything to work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rakovic, it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Before we take the break there's a point Judge Delvoie needs to address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, in the documents you tendered as a package this morning, there is one document that could be a problem. It's document number 65 ter 10110. I didn't notice it immediately because on your initial list it has a regular 65 ter number, I think it was 753, but 10110 indicates that it was not on your 65 ter list. So I have the impression a little bit that it is sneaked in in that list. I'm sure you didn't do it on purpose. But it's a problem, don't you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I don't know the answer to that. I see that on my list I did have a number 753, it's struck through, and now it has another number. I don't know if that's one that was dropped previously and was subject to a motion to add it back in, but if so I don't know when that motion was made, whether it's a pending motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's not subject of a motion to give -- to get it back in. It was not on your motion -- on your last week motion to get documents in, if I'm not wrong. So it's simply not on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see an e-mail now on my case manager's screen from one of my colleagues, who's indicating that we sought to re-instate this document in the motion filed last Friday. It was previously dropped, and he doesn't know why it has a 10.000 series number. So I don't know if the current motion has a request to re-instate 753.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It doesn't. Because if it -- if there would have been such -- if it would be in that motion, I'm afraid it would have -- it would have the same fate as a few other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'll do some research during the break and see what I can find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I'm afraid -- I'm afraid this isn't your lucky day you hoped for a few minutes ago, because we did what Mrs. Korner told us a few days ago our team shouldn't do, that is, double-check the numbers. And we saw that two more documents and documents with apparently normal 65 ter numbers, it is number 160 and 246, are equally not on the 65 ter list. We have not been informed of that, so there's another problem. And now the problem goes to the fact that it is -- that it seems that we can't rely on -- Mrs. Korner assured us that we could rely on the fact that OTP would notify us when a document was not on the 65 ter list and still used in court. But obviously we can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the latest two you mentioned, I have no information to give you at this time. I had no reason to think that they were not on the 65 ter list. I relied on the information that they were. I'll do some further research on those. Can I address specifically 753 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We -- we now saw that it was in the motion, 753.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But with the change of numbers, we didn't address it in the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. May I address that? To what I've been able to learn during the recess is that it was in the motion of last Friday. It was in attachment or annex E, which is a list of documents that had previously been on our list, were removed I think in May of 2008 pursuant to a request or suggestion from the Pre-Trial Judge at the time that we try and reduce our list. It was removed at that time. Then there was a request to re-instate it. I think the way it got the number 10110 was when one of our trial support persons was looking for 753, it didn't appear on the list, so it was -- decided it needed to be assigned a new number to indicate it was a new one. That's where that number came from. First of all, I'd like to assure Your Honour that I didn't do anything like that intentionally. And Mr. O'Sullivan and Mr. Zecevic is not here but, I was in trial with them for two years previously, and I think they will attest for my integrity in regard to something like this. And before I learn the unfortunate news that apparently 160 and 140 are now also a problem, I was going to make a pitch to you for 753 and say this is not one that you decided on in your oral ruling because you didn't know about it, but if I were able to make an argument to you at this point I would ask you to consider allowing the Prosecution to add this one. We think it's relevant. It goes to communications. It's particularly relevant to a point this witness made when he was talking about the classification of urgency in documents. Yesterday when he described the categories from highest to lowest, he described very urgent as the highest and he said he didn't think they ever sent one very urgent out of his centre. This is one that is very urgent, so it's an example. It's one I guess I would use in the way that Judge Harhoff I think suggested to Ms. Korner on a previous occasion, is that just because we've ruled it can't come in, you might use it to confront a witness and ask him if it refreshes his memory or changes his mind about something, So I would propose to use that, but I would ask to use it -- and I would make an argument that in terms of one of the factors you consider in making a decision about that is prejudice to the Defence. This was a document that was on our list back in 2008, they've known about it for some time. We withdrew it. So they might rely on -- I don't need to deal with it. But now that we've added it, they have some time to deal with it, and I would argue that in terms of prejudice and -- one document as opposed to 23 is at least logistically less prejudicial than the 23, and, therefore, it might be a reason for you to make a decision about this one document. I don't have anything to say about the other two yet until I do some further research, and I apologise for this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, we will now continue where we stopped. You gave -- and we were starting to give a very long answer. And you said, as far as I can remember, that the special telephone line was broken down when you talk about the functionality of the communications system, which in essence was the most functional line for the operations of the MUP. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, yesterday you spent quite a lot of time talking about the sending of dispatches or telegrams, and you said that on several occasions you would send some telegrams or dispatches on behalf of the chief. So my question now will be you probably sent those telegrams which were part of your competence, of your line of work; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. I pointed out yesterday, when we addressed somebody with regard to the communications issues such as electricity or post -- postal services, then I used to send dispatches to directors or others in order to try to make these lines secure so that we can operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And of course you had a right to do so in line with the staffing plan and in line with the job descriptions; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood it, and that's what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And these powers come out of the rule book on the public security services, that is the name of your rule book?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was precisely so. I never read anything special with regard to my competences and powers, but that was inherited when I came, and those people who did it before me, they informed me on how I'm supposed to do it afterwards. There were no other barriers, there were no warnings in terms of something that I did wrong or beyond my powers. If I did anything, I always tried to notify somebody else. I always addressed my disposition to people who were supposed to know more about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the CSB system of course there were other sectors and other chiefs who behaved in a similar way. They all operated within their lines of work and within their competences, just like you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. During the proofing and yesterday I looked at several dispatches which were titled -- which were addressed by the chief, and we saw also some signatures by other persons and even headers could have been or from other departments and not from the chiefs, as far as I can recall from looking at several dispatches yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So in principle, when you have a teleprinter officer who is supposed to type in a document, they first read a text and they put a block signature. At that point they're not able to put the addressee?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were only able to put what is written, so they copied it in the -- exactly the same way. Sometimes it was deputy of something, but deputy is not an alternative, it's not what we would consider an alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you put -- when you ticket, you cannot put it in the teleprinter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that can't be done. If there is a document of that type, then it was not done through our communications. It could have been sent through our communications, but it had to be some additional information and some additional initials put on it. But as far as our communications network is concerned, we were not able to send it with a signature. Maybe we were able to send a copy, but that was not usually done through us because we didn't have a copy machine at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the receiving party was only able to see the so-called block signature; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will now show you a document 2D02-1264. Mr. Rakovic, could you please take a careful look at this document. You will probably remember I showed you the minutes from the meeting from the 11th of July. This is from the 24th of July, 1992. Could you please take a look at the number. It is related to your line of work. It is number 11/104.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's 11/104. It seems that it was written in my department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at the signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the signature of the head of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which goes to say and supports what you said before, that it was done on behalf of the head of the centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please take a look at the substance of the document. It says that there should be maximum involvement in maintaining the communications.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We especially pointed out here KT connection communication, which is interesting because it is independent from all other systems. You didn't need to have lots of different cables; you only needed to have a KT station. And that's especially interesting for radio amateurs, for example. We had people who were very well acquainted with radio amateur connections and most police stations did have the KT station, but the KT station was not used to transfer information. That's the essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to stop you here. So you are trying here to say that that kind of system should be established?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We want to establish that kind of system so that if there is some need, that we have this system to transfer some urgent information. That's why we insisted to put in place these KT stations. I remember talking to a chief to prepare a code registry so that it can be distributed to everybody in the field so that information could be transferred through this system. If the person has a code book, then they can decode a particular piece of information. If it's transferred through the so-called free air.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So I assume that before this period this system did not work because you're trying to establish it here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was as if it had existed, but we didn't have people trained to use it. In some stations, in some police stations, which I pointed out in earlier interviews, in some SJBs we had people who were not trained to work on communication issues, and that's why I was forced on my own initiative to send some instructions, that when we recruit new staff, that these people should be first checked by the SJB. And I put up, I set up, a committee. I think there was several people in them so that they can check whether these people had any previous experience because we had cases when people would bring false documents, on which signs they can use in Teletyping and so on. That's why I wanted to have this separate committee so that we can know that these people can use the KT system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So generally speaking, as far as I can see, you tried to set up a communications system to the best of your abilities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, I have a general question with regard to the receipt of documents. So when you would receive a dispatch or a telegram, then it would be registered in a registry book?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a book of incoming dispatches. At the centre itself we had four logs or four books due to a large number of dispatches, to incoming and to outgoing but logs, open and coded, one each.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And dispatches that you received were addressed to different departments within your CSB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly so. If it was, for example, sent to all organisational units and to -- and it could have been addressed to some other services, such as police stations and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And if a document or a dispatch would be addressed to you, then you would get it in your service; if it had been addressed to uniformed police, for example, then they would get it depending on who the addressee was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During working hours we sent dispatches to all addressees. In the afternoon, which is after 3.00 p.m. up until 7.00 a.m., all dispatches which arrived at this period of time, which were sent and were operational in their nature, were sent to operative duty services. And then people from operative duty services, after having read at it, they were able to see who should or should not be notified. That's the way we did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And dispatches were given to addressees through a certain type of signature; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During working hours, employees would take over the dispatch and they would register it into logs and books. In the afternoon if we didn't -- if we had, for example, a dispatch which was not urgent, we talked about different classifications, then we would keep a dispatch if it was not urgent and then we would send it in the morning. Those which are operationally urgent, marked DX, these were sent to operative duty services. And then operative duty services would enter these dispatches into their records, and that means that that was end of our part of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the State Security Service had a special log in which their dispatches were recorded and sent?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the principle was exactly the same. We would receive a dispatch, as from any other service, then we would send it to a particular addressee; or we would receive dispatches from different police stations, and we would forward it to the addressee. And the contact person was usually a secretary of the service, of the State Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, I have a dilemma that you might be able to help me with with regard to two dispatches -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do you want to tender that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hasn't it already been admitted? I will -- I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 2D50, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could look at 65 ter exhibit 478.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, this is a document from the package of documents shown to you by the Prosecutor. It's document dated July the 6th, 1992. It was received but not the entire document was received. I will give you the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You can see here that there was some problems in receiving the document, and there is a part of the document missing as far as I'm able to see.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult to say anything here. Yes, it says 3 and 5 and there's number 4 missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will now give you a hard copy of 65 ter 484 so that you can compare these two. Mr. Rakovic, could you please compare the two. The method is the same, a means of movement through the corridor. It seems to me that it is a dispatch which was not received to the full. Could you please compare the substance of the two documents. So in principle it's the same topic covered by the documents?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only thing that I can see from the first document is that upon the approval of the head of the centre, the head of the communications department - which is myself, which is strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It was strange to me too. There was probably a problem in sending it and that's why a new telegram was sent later?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the 14th of July and the next one is on the 24th of July. Probably, but I'm not sure, is that the first document was supposed to be copied. And then I received an information that it should be revised. So probably upon the approval of the head of the centre I signed it so that the employee could send it. So probably, I assume, the employee sent the entire document, which is the second one. I don't know what happened with the first one. Maybe there was a part missing or there was a part that needed revising. Maybe they didn't receive the entire document and they requested an amendment. First time it was coded, then it was crossed, then some parts were missing. So probably people didn't know what was going on and they wanted a new document to be sent, and I assume I had to contact some people, and from what I learned over the phone I just initialled it, and an employee of mine probably forwarded the entire document afterwards. Because the substance is the same, aside from the point 4 in the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's how I understood it. It's a repeated dispatch or dispatch which was re-sent because the first part was missing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the first part was missing. I never saw these dispatches before, neither during the interview nor during the proofing. This is the first time I have a chance to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, the Prosecutor showed you a document that you spoke to. That's P1102 -- 1002.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have this document on the screen, so P1102.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the first paragraph. Now the chief is talking about illegal actions from some police officers, and there was an event here when a police officer was arrested for murder. There are two police officers mentioned in here. Since you've been shown this from -- by the Prosecutor, do you know anything about this event, and do you know anything about events when police officers were arrested? In paragraph 2, policemen mentioned are Robert Barasanin and Zeljko Bursac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this event. Maybe it was just an event in a range of different events. But if you're asking me whether these things were happening, yes, they were. We did have occasions, I know that, but I have no paperwork which would confirm this case, this specific case. As I said earlier on, dispatches was something I didn't read. I only read dispatches that were sent to me, where I was the addressee. This is a classic, an ordinary dispatch. You can see it was sent from our centre, you can see that some actions were taken with regards to the text during pre-questioning. I just looked visually at the dispatch to see it was derived from. I don't remember the specific case, if that's what you wanted to know. But the actions that were taken were definitely taken. For example, I remember a case from Banja Luka. There was some criminals, with regard to which I talked to somebody and said that criminal does -- goes beyond boundaries of faith or ethnicity. There was a crime that was committed by a Bosnian, Croat, and three Serbs, and I talked to some of ours and I said, "You can see what crime is. Criminals will not fight. They will fight only for the money, not for any other reason."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, in 1992, I'm interested in that part, Stojan Zupljanin never issued instructions which were not compliant with the law or your professional views and principles; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. I performed my activities, which were nothing out of the ordinary. I didn't have any special requests or any special instructions that I had to follow. Everything that I did and everything on which we co-operated was on a technical level that I used to perform. I never got any instructions. We always agreed on what's supposed to be done. That's how it's done even today. I don't take orders from anybody. That's who I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever get an instruction or an order to hide or not show a dispatch?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it never happened. Maybe somebody would tell me that the dispatch was not right, then I would re-send it to be sent back to me in the revised manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rakovic. That completes my questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please ask the usher for his assistance. Please give the witness this binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Rakovic. I'm Slobodan Cvijetic, attorney-at-law, and I'm co-counsel of the Defence team of Mr. Mico Stanisic. I will try to be as brief as possible, and I will try to see what your basic positions are on the communications system in 1992. My foundation for this is what you said during your interview and during your testimony yesterday and today. Could you please keep your comments to whether you agree with what I'm stating or not. Mr. Rakovic, the basis of the communications system of the Ministry of the Interior is the dispatch system and the teleprinter form of communication; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right as far as --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the type of messages concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please pause briefly between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Witness, repeat --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You will have to repeat your answer because you hurried. So could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis was the transmission of a certain type of messages --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All other alternative types of message --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, the interpreters ask that you speak more directly into the microphone because they have a difficulty in hearing what you're actually saying. Thank you. I hope you're comfortable, otherwise the usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, that form of communication, during 1992, you did not actually have it with the centre of security stations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, we did not have that system with the ministry of Republika Srpska, the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Alternative types of communication, such as UKT, KT, telephones, and courier cannot make up for the absence of this basic type of communication if there are problems in their functioning, and you already spoke about that; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: These types of communication, as far as you're concerned, functioned for the most part at local level when they could function, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, especially for UKT communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The basic shortcoming, as far as such communications are concerned, is the lack of security involved; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: An additional problem in 1992 in terms of the functioning of the system of communications with the centre of the ministry lay in the fact that the seat of the centre often moved. So you personally sometimes didn't even know where the centre and the ministry were. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are 100 per cent right. During my term I actually never went to the first territory -- or rather, Bijeljina was the first territory that I went to in terms of where the seat was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, yesterday you looked at a document from the beginning of December 1992, I think it was the 5th of 6th of December. In this document you were asked to give information about the situation regarding the communications system and the problems therein so that an annual report could be compiled at ministry level about the work involved and, among other things, the communications system. Do you remember seeing that document yesterday?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly which document you're referring to exactly. However, the principle involved was the following.
