Always on the eve of the new year there would be a request, or rather, a dispatch stating that organisational units, primarily centres of security services, should prepare a report for the ministry. And the centres of the security services sent this down to their own organisational units so that they could also carry out preparations for compiling an annual report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could the witness please be shown -- or rather, could we see in e-court P625, P625.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, it's number 1 for you. Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at page 36 in B/C/S in e-court. In English it is page 25 and 26. If we cannot have both on the screen at the same time, could we start with 25 and then move on to 26, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, it is page 32 for you. It's not the same page number like in e-court.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the page numbers, F ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Towards the bottom, it's the regular way you mark page numbers. Don't look at the ERN number, it will just confuse you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually you put page numbers on the top of the page, and now I see it here at the bottom, and it's on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I suggest that we deal with this paragraph by paragraph. Do you see what is stated in the first paragraph, "bearing in mind the three basic elements of work of communications and cryptographic data protection." Please be patient and hear me out. "(Personnel technical equipment, and documents). It can be said that this segment of the Ministry of the Interior was among those which initially had the most organisational problems." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is most certainly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please read the next paragraph -- I will actually tell you what it's about. There was a lack of personnel, technical equipment. There weren't proper documents to work with. Response from communications staff was very low, and I think that you talked about that today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So do you agree with this statement made in the report?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree and I spoke of it myself today.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, somebody raised the question of these nodes. So just skip a paragraph now and move on to number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the next page in English on our screens. It says: "Of the central nodes in the MUP ..." Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember there's a reference to nine nodes, and it says that it was only the CSB nodes in Banja Luka and Doboj that remained under Serb control.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. The centre of Bosnia-Herzegovina had Sarajevo as the main node --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just deal with it slowly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The following nodes: Sarajevo was the main node; then there was Gorazde, as far as I can remember; then Tuzla; Zenica; Doboj; Banja Luka; Livno; Bihac; and now I cannot remember whether Bugojno was there or not. Was there a node there? Now, out of all of these nodes the MUP of Republika Srpska had under its control only the Doboj node and the Banja Luka node. Later on, though --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's fine. That will do. In that same paragraph it says that "with the disintegration of the single teleprinter link, the system of cryptographic data protection for written communications in the organs of internal affairs on the territories under our control also disintegrated." Is this true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please skip the KT paragraph. You already discussed that. Let's move on to the next one that says: "There are problems with the UHF network were the lack of radio sets and difficulties ..." et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In B/C/S could we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to repeat what you said about UKT and KT. I'm just asking you to confirm whether this is correct, what was stated about UKT and KT communications.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly, and I already spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Again, if you'd just skip a short paragraph, you have the final statement. "A particular problem for the communications system was the move of the MUP from Vraca to Lukavac, then to Pale and then to Bijeljina." So it was hard to establish a definite communications system until the ministry finally stayed put because it's not easy to move communications system. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. In fact - how should I put this? - we had a system that sort of started operating only when they moved to Bijeljina in 1993, and that is what it says here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this same document, please don't look at the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say this to the Trial Chamber. It is in Serbian page 32 and in English 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's going to be page 28 for you. The page number is at the bottom. The paragraph starts with the following words -- or rather, it's the fourth paragraph in B/C/S -- and perhaps Tanja could help me now and tell me which paragraph it is in the English version. I think it is the second paragraph. It is statistics about the total number of dispatches received at the ministry headquarters, it doesn't say from which centre, but this is the total number. I would just like to deal with the following: If the average daily number of dispatches received was 15, bearing in mind that this came from five centres, bearing in mind the fact that there were two services, namely, the public security service and the national security service, and that they had to send daily reports. So for all other lines of work within the ministry, there would be one dispatch per day. You will agree with me that in war time when things happen very quickly, this is truly insufficient, very little if you bearing in mind that your equipment was overtaxed anyway?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the way it seems. Yes, if you look at the number 15, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And a normal number, that system would have been -- that number would have been much higher if the system were in a different condition?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Could the witness now please be shown document P1010. The 65 ter number is 1264. Have you found this document in your binder? I'm sorry, I'm afraid I've forgotten the number. You'll recognise it from what you see on the screen and then you can find it in your binder. It's number 2. I think it's number 2, the very next document, and then if not -- no, no. 4, 4. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Take a look. It's not that you're unfamiliar with it. You saw it yesterday. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday we made some comments in relation to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please just give me yes or no answers. Mr. Rakovic, this is not a dispatch; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something like this could not be called a dispatch in view of the signatories and --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now have the following document: P1004.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you found this document? You looked at it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it's 15 or 16. I may have got the numbers mixed up. So you saw this document yesterday. Please look at the date, the 4th of May, 1992. Look at it up there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen it. I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And now let's move on to page 2 of the document. You have the signature of Mico Stanisic here. You say you've never seen his signature, but his name is typed there. You will agree with me that this is not a dispatch either. This is a hard copy like the one you see. It's a document, not a dispatch; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We refer to this as a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. That's the proper term. Now, let's have document P1003 on the screen, please. Mr. Rakovic, Mr. Zupljanin evidently received this document, such as it is, refers to it -- he referred to it and then forwarded it to the public security stations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And the date is the 13th of May, 1992, assuming that Mr. Zupljanin, so to say, responded in the usual way and that it took, let's say, 24 hours for this document to be forwarded. Then it can be seen from this that the document travelled for some eight or nine days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I don't want to speculate how the document could have arrived within nine days in that period, but I will put something to you and please listen to me. Don't look at the document anymore. In that initial period in May when there was fighting around the corridor before it was definitely closed, it was possible for someone --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, I'm -- how do you conclude that this document was nine days travelling before it reached its address?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if Mr. Stanisic compiled it on the 4th of May, 1992, and Mr. Zupljanin responded to it on the 13th -- can we continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I am speculating, but let's say somebody managed to carry this physically by hand, risking passing through battle-fields, over mine-fields, and so on and so forth, and now Mr. Zupljanin is forwarding this document, you are forwarding it by means of communication to the SJBs. Along with the problems you had at the local level, or rather, in view of these problems, you certainly would not be able to receive a response within 24 hours, especially not from those SJBs where you had to use alternative means of communication?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you will agree with me that the route followed by this document emanating from the minister would be one where it would take at least a month for a response to take place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, then you will agree that for the functions of a Ministry of the Interior in war time the loss of a month is practically an eternity. It means that communications are not functioning; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not up to me to say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'll just put another general question. I won't show you any more documents. Setting up telephone lines from time to time and establishing communication was done by the postal code service, not by you. You didn't have direct telephone lines with Jahorina, Pale, I'm referring to the MUP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, communications of that sort went through the post office, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So when there was such communication it was through the post office in Sarajevo, and it was insecure because in Sarajevo it could be wire-tapped and it could be cut off; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you certainly are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before we finish today, I do have some additional information about the two documents for Judge Delvoie.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic -- let me find my notes here. At page 15 today Mr. Krgovic was asking you about the total number of dispatches referred to in the six-month report for the first half of the year. You remember that number was something just less than 10.000. And then the number for the three-month period between July and September and that huge difference. And he pointed out the fact that the first three months and maybe another week at the beginning of 1992 were during peacetime, and that may be part of the reason why the number for the first six months was so big. Do you remember that discussion?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that that's what we said today about that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would you agree with me if we had in hand the log-book for received dispatches in Banja Luka, we would be able to look and see how many were received in the first three months of the year and how many in the second three months, and then we'd know precisely what the division was between peacetime and war time during the first half of the year. Would you agree that's where we could find that information?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree that that information would be evident from those books. What books? The dispatch books pertained only to our station. We didn't have those from other stations, so we would have to look at all the dispatches in all the SJBs, collect all this information and --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, let me stop you. I'm only talking about dispatches received in the centre in Banja Luka. Wouldn't that information be in the log-book in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, our dispatches should be there if the books were for the whole year, yes. Well, you know, sir, just let me tell you something --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, I'm sorry, I have limited time. Let me stop you. I think we did show you one log-book from Banja Luka for received documents, but it only starts on 27 November 1992. Do you know whether or not there still exists in the centre of Banja Luka the log-book for received dispatches in 1992 prior to November 27th or where it might be kept today?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that such books are still in existence. They are kept for only a short time because they only serve to prove that we sent or received certain dispatches, and later on they're useless. If we were to keep them, we would have a whole room full of books with no value, containing no useful information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you. You mentioned a number of non-Serbs who were working in the centre in Banja Luka in 1992. Did you know about the body called the ARK Crisis Staff, the Crisis Staff for the Autonomous Region of Krajina, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard about it like I'm hearing from you now. I never knew anything about the existence of this staff or its headquarters. We keep mentioning various staffs. They said there's a staff up there, but it wasn't the staff actually, it was a ministry which had its certain administrative offices and employees. It wasn't a staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, were you not aware of an ARK Crisis Staff decision that called upon the various private and the various business enterprises as well as governmental organisations, including the MUP, to remove non-essential non-Serb personnel? Did you not know about that decision?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be impossible for me to work with some such people, for someone to remove them while I was receiving them. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or rather, employing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were asked at page 33, line 19 today, about the sending of dispatches or telegrams. Did you personally send dispatches or telegrams, actually sit down at the machine and type them up?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You said that you used to send dispatches -- for example, on communication issues, such as electricity or post, you said you used to send dispatches to directors or others. In the MUP and Banja Luka centre, did you have a link to a teleprinter with postal services or any other enterprises in town that were non-MUP?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have such links. We had a telephone link with military headquarters -- or rather, switchboard. We had some with the Territorial Defence in town that was something that was special in our switchboard. We had the Municipal Assembly we could contact, the defence department or whatever it was called. We had five or six local telephone lines linked to our switchboard. We could communicate with the military switchboard, the local post office, and that was to save money.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any Teletype, teleprinter connections with the military or the TO with the VRS or the TO?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not. Our teleprinter system was a closed system. It was not linked up to any external system, any system of another user. Only the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 35, line 11 today you were saying: "But as far as our communications network is concerned, we were not able to send it with a signature. Maybe we were able to send a copy, but that was not done through us because we didn't have a copy machine at that time." Do you mean in your unit, in your communications section, you didn't have a printer? Or did you mean in the whole of the centre of Banja Luka CSB?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the centre the only system we had was a fax machine, 39155 was the number. If we sent a document by fax, there would always be a trace to show what fax the document had some from. Yesterday I viewed several documents here which had no such trace on them. They had a signature on them, but no trace of being sent by fax.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question is: Did you have copier machines in CSB Banja Luka even though you might not have them in your unit's section in the building?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, in our communications centre we never had copy machines and we still don't. Sometimes when I have to make a copy --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay, stop. But didn't you have them in CSB Banja Luka, someplace where you could go and make a copy in the CSB Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection I can't say whether it was 1992. We later had a copy unit downstairs in a small room where people came to get identity cards. There was a copy machine bought and placed there, and the documents would be sent down there for copying. But when I arrived, I really don't remember anyone having a copy machine. I'm sure if someone had had one we would have known about it. In our communications centre there is no copy machine there to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you saying to the best of your memory you never made a copy of a document in 1992 while working at the CSB Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that my staff members and I never had occasion to make a copy of a document. I don't know whether there was a copy machine somewhere else in the building. Perhaps there might have been one in the state security sector where I never went --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but in the parts of the premises where I went, I never saw one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit 2D250.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, this is one that was shown to you by Mr. Krgovic, page 35, line 18 today. And you'll see the number is 11-1/04-76. I think you've explained to us that the 04 means it came from you or your unit, your section. Correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And number 76 would mean that was the 76th dispatch for 1992 from your section, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on this document we see handwritten at the top the name Milos Jankovic. Did you know him in 1992; and if so, where did he work and what did he do?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the gentleman from Cajavec where I worked in 1978. In Prijedor he was chief of the department for communications and cryptographical protection or encryption. It had a department somewhat smaller than our unit. So I assume when the dispatch arrived there because it was addressed to the chief that the Prijedor chief or someone who received the dispatch wrote on it that it should be addressed to Jankovic because he was in charge of encoding in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, how much longer do you think you would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have six notes, so that would be 15 minutes to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we'll take the break and come back in 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Again, for the record, as a matter of courtesy to counsel, I would explain that we were not lollygagging during the extended break, we were working on administrative issues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Just for the record, good afternoon. Mr. Zecevic has joined the Stanisic Defence. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, I was going to sneak in unnoticed, but actually I'm here as well. Joanna Korner joining Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, at page 38 today you were being asked about the operative duty services, and that reminded me. We had seen a few dispatches where the number from the Banja Luka security centre -- security services centre was 11-01/0D and then a number. Now, I know in Serbian there is a word spelled "o-d" which I understand means from. But in the context of a number on an outgoing dispatch I understand OD can mean operative duty. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operative duty service, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic was asking you about 65 ter 478.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could put that up on the screen for the witness quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think this is a document from July the 6th, and it had some information about the opening of the corridor and procedures to be used in connection with that. The handwritten part in the upper right, I wasn't clear, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I just wanted to verify that. And you know there was a -- we looked at a second document that was sent out that had basically the same content as this one, but it had a different number. I think that was 11-1/01-15. If you're re-sending a document, would you use the same number, or did you give it a new number?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had already sent a document which was probably not in good order. And as we sent this the next day, of course the number would be different. That's why we gave it another number because this document is missing a paragraph, paragraph 4, as far as I can see, which is why I even added something on here which means that the employees in my service had re-typed the entire document and probably forwarded it under another number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question, though, is if -- I can understand that if the new document was different, changed, modified, amended, adding something different from the original document, that it should get a new number. If you're simply re-transmitting the exact same document, would it keep the old number, or would that also get a new number? Do you know what the practice was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Evidently that was the practice. Had the practice been different, I probably would have sent it under the same number, but I couldn't send it a few days later with the same number when other numbers had come in between. And of course the document is not identical because an entire passage is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for -- are you saying for the rest of it, it's identical?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see, yes, it is. But the fourth paragraph is missing. That's what I was able to see when I had it before me on the desk, both documents, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we have the documents in. We can take a look at them. I want to move to page 42, line 10 today. You were asked if Mr. Zupljanin ever issued any instructions that weren't compliant with the law or your professional views and principles. You don't know what orders Mr. Zupljanin may have given to other individuals or other units, do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. I know that I never received any orders, either oral or in writing, that might mean I had to do something not in compliance with the law. However, whether he gave any such orders to anybody else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned at page 45, line 4, that Bijeljina was the first territory that you went to in terms of going to the seat or the centre of the RS MUP. Do you recall approximately when it was that you went to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall when it was. All I know is that my first visit to the MUP line of work where we had a meeting organised by Mr. Dragan Kezunovic, and it took place in Bijeljina, but what month this was I'm not sure. It was probably 1993 because I think that's when the MUP headquarters were moved to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that meeting was with Mr. Kezunovic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the chief of the administration for communications and encryption, and he was the one who convened the meeting. I know I attended that meeting. I remember that Mr. Kezunovic had a bed in one of the offices where he slept, and we practically had our meeting in his bedroom. The colleagues from the other centres would come there and that's where we had our meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sounds like another STA I know. But where -- what was the purpose of this meeting, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the usual sort of meeting about the situation as regards communications; about procurement of equipment, whether one could get something somewhere; how to improve communications. That first meeting was also for me to introduce myself to other people and get to know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. At page 48, line 16, today you mentioned -- or you agreed that one of the particular problems for communications systems was the move of the seat of the MUP or the centre of the MUP from Vraca to Lukavac and then to Pale and then to Bijeljina. Did you have any mobile units with Teletype or teleprint machines in them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in the MUP headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I mean in the MUP, whether it was in Banja Luka or at the SJBs, anywhere in the MUP, did you have that kind of equipment? Did you have mobile units which included Teletype machines, teleprinter, Teletype machines?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't fully understand the question. We -- whether we in our headquarters had all this, we did, but in the headquarters of the MUP, which was in Lukavica or Pale. As I didn't go up there, I don't know whether they had -- what equipment they had. I didn't see it myself. We had what we had. And in the annual report of 1992 we, like all the other stations, sent our report. So we said we have a teleprinter, TG1 and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. The point that I'm trying to make is that the MUP in 1992 did possess mobile communication machines -- mobile communication units, which included Teletype/teleprinter machines; is that right? You may not know how many or exactly where they were located, but they did exist within the MUP in 1992, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I he see Mr. Cvijetic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I think that it's a leading question. It is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Technically Mr. Cvijetic is correct, but I don't see a problem with the question. Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you understand my question, sir? Did you have that kind of equipment in the MUP in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what, you asked me whether the ministry had such equipment. The ministry did, and we were part of the ministry. Now, whether the ministry up there in headquarters --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, as I say, I didn't even know where it was, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you aware that there was a mobile unit with a Teletype printer in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prijedor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one or two final questions. At page 50 today, I think Mr. Cvijetic showed you a document, 65 ter 1264. That was the document from Mr. Gajic, I believe. Do you recall that one?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall it was shown yesterday and today.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you were asked if that were a dispatch. You said: "No, something like this could not be called -- could not be called a dispatch in view of the signatories," but that document is something from which a dispatch could be prepared, was it not? It had a number, it had a date.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to all of that, it might have, but the way it was done, it does not look like a dispatch. I pointed out yesterday that I didn't even know that there was that kind of department, a department for mobilisation at the centre. It said there that he was head of some department, this or that, whatever. I know for that reason that that kind of thing could not pass as it were because it did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, as far as you know it didn't exist, correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we look at P1004, 1004. This is the last document I'm going to ask you about, sir. Mr. Cvijetic showed you this and asked you what this was, and you indicated that it was a -- it was not a dispatch. You said: "We referred to this as a document."

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, because I had a look at the first and the second page. If I were only to look at the first page -- well, I mean, just a piece of paper on which something was written. It might be a dispatch had it been delivered through our system, however it could not been sent through our system. I did not see a stamp, a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to the second page or the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, is there any reason that if this had been presented in the communications centre in this form, that it could not be converted to a dispatch? You have a number, you see who it's coming from, you see who it's supposed to go to. It simply needs to be mechanically transposed into a document that can be sent out on the Teletype, right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying once again, this kind of text, I mean to put it on a teleprinter machine and to re-type it, it would be a dispatch and it would leave without a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, I'm saying it's not a dispatch for the following reason because probably --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I understand. Thank you. You've answered all my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm finished, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. However, during the re-direct on page 54, page 7, the witness started answering a question and then the Prosecutor interrupted him. I think that it would be right to allow the witness to finish that answer. Could the Trial Chamber allow me to ask the witness so that he could finish giving the answer because it has to do with what we've been discussing today. So may I be allowed to put that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Krgovic. Further cross-examination by Mr. Krgovic:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Rakovic, when you were answering the Prosecutor's question and when he asked you whether you could establish the number of received dispatches only on the basis of log-book in Banja Luka of dispatches received and sent, you said that in order to answer you would have to have the books from the public security stations; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sorry, we have a time problem. So this number of 9.000 that is mentioned here, that is the total number of received and sent dispatches for all the public security stations and the centre?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, in the territory of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when we're talking about received and sent dispatches, some of them are recorded at the public security station as received, and at the centre they're registered as sent, but they're actually one in the same dispatch; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. That is all I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, on document exhibited as P -- about P1004, the last document you were asking questions about to the witness. If I understood well the witness said, this is not -- you said, sir, this is not a dispatch, and I can't recognise this as something that was processed through our service. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Doesn't it follow from that, Mr. Hannis, that this document could not be admitted through this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. This is -- this is inextricably intertwined with the dispatch from Banja Luka CSB which was forwarding the contents of P1004, and it made explicit reference to it by date and by number. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My argument is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I've got your point. I've got your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I'm satisfied. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Rakovic, thank you for your testimony. The core of your testimony yesterday and today has been to give us an impression of the possibilities of the CSB in Banja Luka to communicate with the SJBs within its area. And you have told us on the one hand that the communication lines were extremely difficult, at certain times even impossible. And in your many answers to the questions put by the Defence counsels, you have testified that during the war, that is to say after the breakout of armed conflict in April 1992, it was at times extremely difficult to communicate from the CSB to the SJBs around in the region because of the telephone lines were broken, because of the cuts in power, no electricity, because of the danger of travelling by road to have a person transmitting the message, and because of also the malfunctioning of your equipment. What you had at your disposal was simply not working and had needed to be repaired and fixed all the time. So all of this together made communications extremely difficult. Yet, the Prosecution has told us and has shown and you have confirmed that, that a great number of communications were actually transmitted, at a minimum I think about a thousand communications every month, even at the minimum, sometimes perhaps even more. So there seems to be a contradiction somehow between the two parts of your testimony, and this is what my question is about. How are we to reconcile the fact that on the one hand, in fact, a great number of communications were able to get through the lines, and yet on the other hand your testimony that communications were impossible? So can you clarify exactly to give us a better impression of the ability of the CSB to follow what was going on in the SJBs and the ability of the SJBs to report back to the SSB [sic] of what was happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. Both things that I said were correct. I said that it was made more difficult, yes. It became more difficult because of all the reasons that you mentioned and there was yet another one. There were usual directions in which communications evolved, and those were cut off. And it's not only that. For example, all the western Krajina municipalities were -- became part of the SJB, and they were connected only with Livno and Bihac. Telecom and PTT lines did not exist there, cables and the like, and that created a problem for us. It is correct that we did manage to establish quite a few communications with stations that were closer to us and that remained intact, if I can put it that way. Then the equipment, the transmission equipment was there, relatively speaking. Sometimes we'd have devices without having documents. We did not have documents that were coming in regularly. There were old documents that became unusable because they were printed, they were made for the old system. So we could not even use some of the existing documents. Therefore, it was not only a question of lack of equipment. It was also a lack of documents, of directions, cables, et cetera. I remember when the PTT were placing relays on different elevations and then our communications became combined, partly radio relay, partly cable. And then again only cable, and that is how these communications went. It is true that, for example, for a few days there wouldn't be telephone connections with some destinations; however, time was required to establish communications and to get this done. If we say 1.000 dispatches for about 20 stations that were covered by Banja Luka in 30 days, that doesn't really mean anything, two or three. For example, there would be one dispatch by way of regular information. That was really not much of a number, as would be required in view of all the things that were happening at that time. Therefore, I can claim that the communications system was collapsing. That is a fact. I told you yesterday as well, and I'm saying it again today, we would establish communication in the morning. We could work but then we could not work because the station that we were supposed to send the dispatch to had no electricity. When they would get electricity, then we would have no electricity. That kind of thing happened. Then the dispatch would not arrive on time. The destination would be written on the top of the document, it would say "to all police stations," but perhaps only five would receive it. Once they arrive in the territory, they're treated as 20 arrived dispatches. Every station gets one dispatch, and we would just be sending one dispatch but it would go to five different destinations, for instance. I don't know. I mean, I don't see that there is any kind of special collision involved. I mean, you can ask me something specific if you like. From all these reports and the report of the ministry that we looked at a few moments ago, you can see what the situation actually was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I didn't mean to suggest that you have been contradicting yourself. The question that I put to you was merely that the two parts of your testimony would seem to be somehow at odds, and I was actually just asking you to explain, and you have given a good answer to my question. Could I clarify by asking you what possibilities were available to you if you were trying to send an important dispatch to an SJB somewhere within your area of responsibility and you discovered that you couldn't do it because the recipient had no power? What would you do then? Would you then try to send the dispatch to another SJB nearby and ask them to see if they could bring it over to the final destination somehow, or how did you cope with these things, with these shortcomings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely just as you put it. Sometimes we could not send it. Sometimes the machine would break down at the receiving station. That kind of thing happens to this day. Then we would of course ask the nearest police station where the equipment was functioning to receive the dispatch and then for them to send it on. We can say that there were such cases, yes, and then sometimes we would wait. I told you, for example, in the morning we would try to send it. It would be logged in in the book in the morning because it says "to all SJBs." And then he would tick off the ones that he managed to send them to and then his colleague would come for the next shift and he would say, "See, these dispatches could not have been sent." Now if these were urgent dispatches, then he would have to inform the sending party of the dispatch that the dispatch had not actually been sent, and we don't know what would happen after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were you aware of situations in which urgent dispatches never left -- never got out of this -- of your department in the CSB? In other words, were there situations where something that should have been sent out, in the end never was sent out because for one or the other reason it turned out to be impossible and in the end the dispatch was never sent? Were there such situations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGO RAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that there were such situations. However, as for myself personally, since I had a head of department for information transmission and for crypto protection, that person worked more on that kind of thing. Sometimes he would not even inform me about it. He would contact the party sending the dispatch, contact them directly. So it's not that something special would happen. I mean, then he would tell me about it too if there were a standstill. But this kind of thing happened every day, so they had to deal with such problems on a daily basis. There was the person in charge of dispatches who took care of all these dispatches. I mean, I never came close to that kind of thing. No one would come and tell me and say, "A dispatch to such and such a place was not sent." That would be a very special situation that they would call me and that I would have to look into the matter. I mean, the man in charge there, he would look at it and he would see whether there was any other possibility, he would inform the sending party that it was impossible to send this dispatch, things like that. If I tell you that there was no need for me to go there, I mean, I'd go there very rarely. Basically I didn't even walk in there where they worked on dispatches. Sometimes I went there to see who was there but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rakovic, for your assistance to the Tribunal. You are now released as a witness and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. The usher will escort you from the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We in the meantime understood that the two last documents we were talking about, that there was only an error in numbering or a problem in numbering, but they were actually on your 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, so that problem is solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: As for your -- for the document 10110 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- or 753, whatever, we took into consideration, the Trial Chamber took into consideration your application. And we decide that in the interest of justice it may be added to the 65 ter list so that we don't have to do anything special about the exhibit list. It stays -- it is exhibited and it stays exhibited.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour, and I appreciate that. And for the record I would just add in terms of evaluating prejudice to the Defence, it was one of the 14 documents I notified them I wanted to seek to admit and there was no objection. I'm not trying to sneak that past them, but that was just a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think we need to go into private session for the administrative matters that now arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's something I wish to raise, but it can be done in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in connection with a witness who was discussed in closed session, on the 19th of February, 2010, the OTP sent an e-mail asking for replacement of certain documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You do realise we're in open session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you want to discuss a witness who testified in closed session --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just the documents, not the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Your Honour, I think if the witness testified in closed session, then we ought to have this discussion in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We'll go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, you through the misunderstandings and the difficulties about documents being on the 65 ter list or not, the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that it would be very useful if we could have a consolidated 65 ter list with all the indications of what's on and what's off, et cetera. We would like this list -- we would like to agree an Excel format with your services for this list on the basis of the list you used for -- to notify documents to use with each and every witness with some suggestions we might have. Could it eventually be possible that someone of our team meets your case manager to see what can be done and what would be too much to ask?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm not quite clear on that. We can certainly indeed -- it's something we ourselves, you won't be surprised to hear as a result of the last few witnesses we're considering -- we are going to give Your Honours an electronic version of the 65 ter list without all the -- this was taken -- ours at the moment looks -- it has entries saying this was taken off, this is being re-instated. We think ourselves it would be useful for Your Honours, and we will provide it to the Defence as well, to have a complete electronic list. Is that what Your Honour is asking for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we have maybe some suggestions for that list, how it could be improved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Well, Your Honour, we're always happy to entertain anything that helps us not have these considerable discussions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If Your Honours' Legal Officers make an appointment -- not make an appointment, arrange, we'll do it with the case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May we be included in that communication as well, in a sense that we at least know in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Of the list or of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of the list, yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Or the improvement of the list as well.

utterances.text: Your Honours, we might as well deal with this now. We've got five minutes. Can we get back to private session, please.
